title: The Web Needs an Agent Entrance

audience.priorKnowledge: Uses AI coding tools and understands APIs, forms, web apps, and basic security tradeoffs. New to Agent Cards, structured handoff, encrypted intake, and adaptive attendee decks.
audience.desiredOutcome: Can explain why services need an agent-native entrance next to the human UI, and can inspect deck.json as the source of truth.

corePromise: Every serious service will need an agent-native entrance beside the human UI, and semantic live decks make that shift explainable without becoming a full presentation platform.

slides.title: The user already told their agent
slides.speakerIntent: Make the audience feel the waste in asking a user to retype data their agent already prepared.
slides.attendeeTakeaway: The human web flow becomes incomplete when a personal agent is doing the preparation.

content.headline: The form still asks the human to start over.
bullets: The user gave their agent the goal and context.
The service only exposes labels and fields for a browser user.
The final mile becomes copy-paste instead of handoff.

slides.notes: Start concrete. Do not mention protocols yet. Use the image of a user watching their agent prepare everything, then being asked to type it again.

slides.title: Human UI is not a protocol
slides.speakerIntent: Show why browser automation is useful but fragile when it becomes the only agent path.
slides.attendeeTakeaway: Scraping a human interface is brittle, hidden, and hard to audit.

content.headline: Agents need more than pixels and labels.
bullets: Layout changes break task automation.
Hidden assumptions are hard for users to inspect.
Manual fallback turns the agent into a clipboard.

slides.notes: Keep this balanced. Browser agents are useful. The claim is that services should expose a cleaner path when the task matters.

slides.title: Two bad choices
slides.speakerIntent: Give the audience a simple mental model for the broken default.
slides.attendeeTakeaway: Scrape the form or make the user copy-paste are both weak defaults.

content.headline: Scrape the page, or make the user do the work.

slides.notes: This is the first punchline. Let the contrast breathe before introducing the additive shape.

slides.title: Keep the human UI. Add an agent entrance.
slides.speakerIntent: Make the product shape feel additive, not anti-human.
slides.attendeeTakeaway: The answer is a service-owned agent path beside the human interface.

content.headline: The next web has two doors.
bullets: Humans still inspect, override, and complete tasks directly.
Agents get a discoverable path for structured handoff.
The service owns the contract instead of hoping layout automation works.

slides.notes: Say this sentence slowly. This is the line the audience should remember after the talk.

slides.title: Minimum useful agent entrance
slides.speakerIntent: Show the smallest system that is useful without sounding like a giant platform.
slides.attendeeTakeaway: Discovery, schema, consent, verification, and fallback are the core pieces.

content.headline: Boring is the feature.
bullets: A discoverable card tells agents what the service accepts.
A structured intake request carries schema and consent.
A secure submission path lets the service verify the handoff.
A human-readable fallback keeps the user in control.

slides.notes: Use this slide to lower the temperature. The MVP is not replacing websites. It is making a narrow handoff reliable.

slides.title: The deck follows the same rule
slides.speakerIntent: Explain why this deck is semantic before showing files.
slides.attendeeTakeaway: Do not trap meaning in rendered output when another agent needs to adapt it later.

content.headline: Pixels are the presentation, not the source of truth.
bullets: The speaker view is one rendering.
The attendee view is another rendering.
Personalized views should consume semantic slide data.

slides.notes: Bridge from web services to decks. The analogy is the point: structured handoff beats reverse engineering.

slides.title: Four artifacts, one source
slides.speakerIntent: Give the audience concrete files to look for in the published package.
slides.attendeeTakeaway: deck.json is the durable source. HTML files are renderings.

content.headline: Inspect deck.json first.
bullets: deck.json: semantic slide IR and source of truth.
speaker.html: delivery view with notes, timing, and navigation.
speaker-notes.md: script, timing, branches, and handoff cues.
attendee.html: standalone reader view for people after the talk.

slides.notes: Open the generated folder here. Point at purpose, speakerIntent, attendeeTakeaway, and adaptationHints in deck.json.

slides.title: The trust model is scoped handoff
slides.speakerIntent: Prevent the audience from hearing this as 'let agents do anything'.
slides.attendeeTakeaway: The safe version is scoped discovery, explicit consent, structured payloads, verification, and fallback.

content.headline: Not unlimited agent power. Clear boundaries.
bullets: Discovery says what is possible.
Consent says what the user allowed.
Structured payloads say what was sent.
Service-side verification says what was accepted.

slides.notes: This is the risk slide. Keep it precise. Do not overclaim security properties that are not in the current package.

slides.title: The next web has an entrance for agents
slides.speakerIntent: End with the thesis and a concrete next inspection step.
slides.attendeeTakeaway: Keep the human UI, but give agents a service-owned entrance with structured handoff and consent.

content.headline: Keep the human UI. Give agents a clean entrance.
bullets: The user stays in control.
The service owns the contract.
The agent gets a path that does not depend on guessing the page.

slides.notes: Repeat the exact one-sentence takeaway. Then point the audience to deck.json as the artifact that makes later personalization possible.
